To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
rotavirus RNAs with exposed, uncapped 5’ ends activate innate immune signaling in mammalian cells, and that these RNAs contain both capped and uncapped species.
rotavirus infection activates the RIG-I pathway of innate immunity through the production of RNAs that are uncapped, contain exposed 5’ phosphates and are 2’-OMe deficient.
rotavirus RNAs activate innate immune signaling by exposing RIG-I and to some extent MDA5, through the production of uncapped and partially methylated viral RNAs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms by which rotavirus induces the innate immune response in mammalian cells.
the mechanisms that rotavirus uses to evade the innate immune response and establish a successful infection in the human intestine.
understanding the mechanisms that control innate immune activation by rotavirus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

rotavirus RNAs with exposed phosphate groups at their 5’ ends, and RNAs with 2’- O-methylated 2’-hydroxyl groups at their 3’ ends, are capable of activating innate immune signaling through RIG-I. This
rotavirus replication results in the production of uncapped, partially capped, or 2’O-methylated capped RNAs that are potent IFN inducer.
this thesis describes the identification and characterization of rotaviral RNA species that activate innate immune sensing and signaling.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the innate immune signaling by rotavirus is not only dependent on the viral double-stranded RNA but also on the presence of uncapped RNA species with exposed 5' phosphate groups.
rotavirus RNAs activate innate immune signaling in a manner that involves the RIG-I pathway.
rotavirus infection induces innate immunity in a manner that is distinct from other positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
rotaviruses are not as good as other RNA viruses at avoiding detection by host innate immune sensors.

rotavirus, a virus that is not known to be associated with any disease of the central nervous system, can nevertheless induce innate immune signaling through a mechanism that is not completely understood.
rotavirus, like other RNA viruses, produces a variety of RNAs with different structural features that can activate the innate immune response.
